<!-- conj-1: body_md -->
\label{BCconj} (the {\bf Baum-Connes conjecture}) For $i=0,1$, the assembly map 
\begin{equation}\label{BCstandard}
\mu_G: K_i^G(\underline{E}G)\rightarrow K_i(C^*_r(G))
\end{equation}
is an isomorphism.
<!-- end conj-1 -->
<!-- def-1: body_md -->
The reduced $C^*$-algebra $C^*_r(G)$ is the norm closure of $\lambda_G(L^1(G))$ in the bounded operators on $L^2(G)$.
<!-- end def-1 -->
<!-- ex-1: body_md -->
\label{abelian1} If $G$ is abelian with Pontryagin dual $\hat{G}:=Hom(G,S^1)$, then by Fourier transform $C^*_r(G)$ identifies with $C_0(\hat{G})$, the continuous function vanishing at infinity on $\hat{G}$.
<!-- end ex-1 -->
<!-- def-2: body_md -->
For $A$ a unital $C^*$-algebra: $$K_1(A):=\lim_{\longrightarrow} U_n(A)/U_n(A)^0.$$
<!-- end def-2 -->
<!-- ex-2: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $A=\mathbb{C}$, the unitary group $U_n(\mathbb{C})$ is connected, hence $K_1(\mathbb{C})=0$.
\item For $A=C(S^1)$, the continuous functions over the circle, the winding number $w:GL_1(C(S^1))\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$ induces an isomorphism $GL_1(C(S^1))/GL_1(C(S^1))^0\simeq\mathbb{Z}$. Composing with the determinant, we have that $w\circ\det$ induces an isomorphism $GL_n(C(S^1))/GL_n(C(S^1))^0\simeq\mathbb{Z}$. Finally $K_1(C(S^1))=\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end ex-2 -->
<!-- def-3: body_md -->
For $A$ a non-unital $C`*$-algebra: $K_1(A):=K_1(A^+)$ where $A^+$ denotes the unitization of $A$.
<!-- end def-3 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{K1abelian} The group $K_1(A)$ is abelian.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- exo-1: body_md -->
Verify that, if the projections $p,q\in M_n(A)$ are unitarily conjugate, then $p\sim q$.
<!-- end exo-1 -->
<!-- def-4: body_md -->
For $A$ a unital $C^*$-algebra, $K_0(A)$ is the Grothendieck group of the commutative monoid $Proj(M_\infty(A))/\sim$.
<!-- end def-4 -->
<!-- ex-3: body_md -->
\label{ExK0}\begin{enumerate}
\item For $A=\mathbb{C}$, a projection in $M_\infty(\mathbb{C})$ is characterized up to equivalence by its rank, so $Proj(M_\infty(\mathbb{C}))/\sim$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{N},+$. Kence $K_0(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{Z}$.
\item If $X$ is a compact space\footnote{For us, being compact implies being Hausdorff.}, and $A=C(X)$, the $C^*$-algebra of continuous functions on $S$, then by the Serre-Swan theorem $K_0(C(X))$ identifies with $K^0(X)$, the Grothendieck group of the commutative monoid of isomorphism classes of complex vector bundles over $X$. In particular, if $X$ is contractible every vector bundle over $X$ is trivial and $K_0(C(X))=\mathbb{Z}$.
\item Consider $X=S^1$: of course $S^1$ is not contractible, however every {\it complex} vector bundle over $S^1$ is trivial\footnote{This would not be true for {\it real} vector bundles over $S^1$, as shown by the open M\"obius band.}.  Indeed, let $E$ be a complex vector bundle over $S^1$, say of rank $n\geq 1$. View $S^1$ as the quotient of $[0,1]$ by identiying endpoints, let $p:[0,1]\rightarrow S^1$ denote the quotient map. As $[0,1]$ is contractible, the pull-back vector bundle $p^*E$ is trivial. So $E$ is described by the identification of the fibre at 0 with the fibre at 1, i.e. by some element $A\in GL_n(\mathbb{C})$. But by connectedness of $GL_n(\mathbb{C})$ we may homotope $A$ to the identity, making $E$ isomorphic to the trivial bundle. As a result $K_0(C(S^1))=\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end ex-3 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
\label{idem/proj} Assume that, instead of dealing with projections to define $K_0(A)$, we relax the condition of being self-adjoint, and just work with idempotent elements. So let $Idem(M_\infty(A))$ denote the set of idempotents in $M_\infty(A)$; say that idempotents $e,f\in M_n(A)$ are equivalent $(e\sim' f$) if there exist $u,v\in M_n(A)$ such that $e=vu,\; f=uv$. We claim that the monoid $Proj(M_\infty(A))/\sim$ and $Idem(M_\infty(A))/\sim'$ are actually the same. The reason is that any idempotent in a unital $C^*$-algebra is equivalent to a projection. Here is a short proof (taken from \cite{FaMa}): if $e\in A$ is idempotent, define a positive element:
$$z=1+(e^*-e)^*(e^"-e) = 1-(e^*-e)^2=1-e-e^*+ee^*+e^*e.$$
Then $z$ is invertible and $ze=ez=ee^*e$. So $z$ and $z^{-1}$ commute with $e$ and $e^*$. Set then
$$p:=ee^*z^{-1}.$$
Then $p\in Proj(A)$ (check that $p=p^2$; actually $p$ is the support projection of $e^*$). Finally $ep=p$ trivially while $pe= z^{-1}ee^*e=z^{-1}ze=e$, so $e\sim' p$. So using idempotents rather than projections defines the same group $K_0(A)$. This remark will be useful in Proposition \ref{traceKth}.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- def-5: body_md -->
For $A$ a non-unital $C^*$-algebra, define $$K_0(A):=\ker[\epsilon_*:K_0(A^+)\rightarrow K_o(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{Z}].$$
<!-- end def-5 -->
<!-- conj-2: body_md -->
\label{KapKad} (Kaplansky-Kadison, around 1954) If $G$ is torsion-free, then the only idempotents in $C^*_r(G)$ are 0 and 1.
<!-- end conj-2 -->
<!-- ex-4: body_md -->
Assume $G$ abelian. Then $\hat{G}$ is a compact abelian group, and $C^*_r(G)=C(\hat{G})$ (see Example \ref{abelian1}). So $C^*_r(G)$ has no non-trivial idempotent if and only if $\hat{G}$ is connected; by Pontryagin duality, this happens if and only if $G$ is torsion-free.
<!-- end ex-4 -->
<!-- ex-5: body_md -->
\label{torsiongivesidem} Assume $G$ has torsion, i.e. there exists $g\in G$ with finite order $N\geq 2$. Then $p_g:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\lambda_G(g^k)$ is a non-trivial projection in $C^*_r(G)$. So the assumption in Conjecture \ref{KapKad} is necessary.
<!-- end ex-5 -->
<!-- def-6: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $C^*$-algebra. A {\bf trace} on $A$ is a continuous linear functional $\tau$ on $A$ such that $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ for every $a,b\in A$. A trace $\tau$ is {\bf positive} if $\tau(a^*a)\geq 0$ for every $a\in A$. A positive trace $\tau$ is {\bf faithful} if $\tau(a^*a)=0$ implies $a=0$. If $A$ is unital, a trace $\tau$ is {\bf normalized} if $\tau(1_A)=1$.
<!-- end def-6 -->
<!-- ex-6: body_md -->
On $C^*_r(G)$, we have the {\bf canonical trace} $\tau_G(a):=\langle a(\delta_e)|\delta_e\rangle$ for $a\in C^*_r(G)$. It is normalized (clear), positive ($\tau_G(a^*a)=\|a(\delta_e)\|_2^2\geq 0$), and faithful. To check the letter, let $\rho_G$ denote the right regular representation of $G$ on $\ell^2(G)$, and observe that $\rho(G)$ commutes with $C^*_r(G)$. Then, if $a\in C^*_r(G)$ is such that $a(\delta_e)=0$, we have for all $g\in G$:
$$0=\rho(g^{-1})a(\delta_e)=a\rho(g^{-1})(\delta_e)=a(\delta_g);$$
so $a$ vanishes on a basis of $\ell^2(G)$, hence $a=0$.
<!-- end ex-6 -->
<!-- exo-2: body_md -->
Check that $\tau_G$ is indeed a trace on $C^*_r(G)$.
<!-- end exo-2 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{traceKth} Let $A$ be a $C^*$-algebra with unit $1_A$, and $\tau$ be a trace on $A$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There exists a homomorphism $\tau_*:K_0(A)\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that $\tau_*[1_A]=\tau(1_A)$.
\item If $\tau$ is positive, then $\tau_*(K_0(A))\subset\mathbb{R}$.
\item If $\tau$ is positive, faithful, normalized, and $\tau_*(K_0(A))=\mathbb{Z}$, then $A$ has no non-trivial idempotent. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- conj-3: body_md -->
\label{Integraltrace} (Integrality of the trace) If $G$ is torsion-free, then $$(\tau_G)_*(K_0(C^*_r(G)))=\mathbb{Z}.$$
<!-- end conj-3 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{BaumDouglas} If $G$ is torsion-free, then $$(\tau_G)_*(\mu_G(K_0^G(\underline{E}G)))=\mathbb{Z}.$$
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
If $G$ is torsion-free and $\mu_G$ is onto, then Conjecture \ref{Integraltrace} holds. In particular, Conjecture \ref{BCconj} implies Conjecture \ref{Integraltrace}.
$\blacksquare$
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
This proof will allow to get a first feeling of the LHS of Conjecture \ref{BCconj}. Let $BG$ be a classifying space for $G$, i.e. a CW-complex with fundamental group $G$ such that the universal cover $EG:=\widetilde{BG}$ is contractible\footnote{Topologists also say that $BG$ is a $K(G,1)$-Eilenberg-MacLane space, or an aspherical space with fundamental group $G$.}; such a space $BG$ always exists and is unique up to homotopy; see also Example \ref{universalex} below. Since $G$ is torsion-free, we may take $\underline{E}G=EG$, and since $G$ acts freely on $EG$ we have 
$$K_i^G(\underline{E}G)=K_i(BG)$$
for $i=0,1$.  Now, as we will see in Definition \ref{LHS}:
$$K_i(BG)=\lim_{X\subset BG} KK_i(C(X),\mathbb{C}),$$
where the limit is on the directed set of compact subsets $X$ in $BG$, and $KK_i$ denotes Kasparov bivariant K-theory (see subsection \ref{KKordinary}); for $A$ a $C^*$-algebra, $K_i(A,\mathbb{C})$ is the analytical $K$-homology of $A$, see \cite{HiRo}.

By a result of P. Baum and R.G. Douglas \cite{BaDo}, an element $x\in KK_0(C(X),\mathbb{C})$ can be described as a quadruple $(M,E,D,f)$ such that 
\begin{itemize}
\item $M$ is a smooth closed manifold (i.e. compact without boundary).
\item $E=E^+\oplus E^-$ is a smooth vector bundle over $M$.
\item $D:C^\infty(M,E^\pm)\rightarrow C^\infty(M,E^\mp)$ is an elliptic differential operator acting on smooth sections of $E^\pm$.
\item $f:M\rightarrow X$ is a continuous map.
\end{itemize}
At this point we observe that the triple $(M,E,D)$ defines an element $y\in KK_0(C(M),\mathbb{C})$ such that $f_*(y)=x$. Ellipticity of $D$ guarantees that the spaces $Ker(D)$ and $Coker(D)$ are finite-dimensional, so we have the Fredholm index (see Definition \ref{Fred} below):
$$Ind(D):=\dim_\mathbb{C} Ker(D)-\dim_\mathbb{C} Coker(D)$$
that defines the index map $Ind: KK_0(C(M),\mathbb{C})\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$.

Now form the pull-back
$$\left.\begin{array}{ccc}\tilde{M} & \rightarrow & EG \\ p\downarrow &  & \downarrow \\M & \stackrel{f}{\rightarrow} & BG\end{array}\right.$$
so that $\tilde{M}$ is a proper $G$-manifold. Let $\tilde{E}:=p^*E$ denote the pulled-back vector bundle, and $\tilde{D}$ the lift of $D$, so that $\tilde{D}$ is a $G$-invariant elliptic differential operator acting on sections of $\tilde{E}$. Since $\tilde{M}$ is non-compact as soon as $G$ is infinite, classical ellipticity theorems fail, and $Ker(\tilde{D}),\,Coker(\tilde{D})$ are usually infinite-dimensional. However $Ker(\tilde{D}),\,Coker(\tilde{D})$  are modules over $C^*_r(G)$ and it is a result by A. Connes and H. Moscovici \cite{CoMo} that the formal difference of those modules provides a well-defined element $Ind_G(\tilde{D})$, called the $G$-index of $\tilde{D}$, in the K-theory of the reduced $C^*$-algebra\footnote{Although this is not true, one may morally think that $Ker(\tilde{D}),\,Coker(\tilde{D})$ are finitely generated projective modules over $C^*_r(G)$.}. Moreover 
$$Ind_G(\tilde{D})=\mu_G(x).$$
By Atiyah's $L^2$-index theorem (see \cite{Ati}):
$$(\tau_G)_*(Ind_G(\tilde{D}))=Ind(D),$$
which amounts to saying that the following diagram is commutative:
$$\left.\begin{array}{ccc}KK_0(C(M),\mathbb{C}) & \stackrel{\mu_G}{\longrightarrow} & K_0(C^*_r(G)) \\ & & \\Ind\downarrow&  & \downarrow(\tau_G)_* \\ & & \\ \mathbb{Z} & \hookrightarrow & \mathbb{R}\end{array}\right.$$
The result is now clear. $\blacksquare$
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- conj-4: body_md -->
\label{Whitehead} Assume that $G$ admits a 2-dimensional model for $BG$. Then any invertible $T\in GL_n(A)$ is stably homotopic to a $N$-by-$N$ diagonal matrix
$$\left(\begin{array}{ccccc}g & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\0 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1\end{array}\right)$$
for some $N\geq n$ and some $g\in G$.
<!-- end conj-4 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
Assume that $G$ admits a 2-dimensional $BG$, and $\mu_G$ is onto. Then Conjecture \ref{Whitehead} holds.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
As $G$ is discrete, the canonical map
$$G\rightarrow C^*_r(G):g\mapsto\lambda_G(g)$$
embeds $G$ into the unitary group $U_1(C^*_r(G))$. Composing with the canonical map $U_1(C^*_r(G))\rightarrow K_1(C^*_r(G))$, and using commutativity of $K_1$ (Proposition \ref{K1abelian}), we get the canonical map $\iota:G/[G,G]\rightarrow K_1(C^*_r(G))$.

Since $G$ is torsion-free, as in the proof of Proposition \ref{BaumDouglas} , the  LHS of Conjecture \ref{BCconj} can be replaced by $K_i(BG)$. As $BG$ is 2-dimensional, we have a Chern character $Ch_*:K_1(BG)\rightarrow H_1(BG,\mathbb{Z})$ which is an isomorphism, where $H_1$ denotes the usual cellular homology. Moreover the following diagram is commutative (see e.g. \cite{Matthey}):
$$\left.\begin{array}{ccc}K_1(BG) & \stackrel{\mu_G}{\longrightarrow} & K_1(C^*_r(G) \\ &  &  \\Ch_*\downarrow &  & \uparrow\iota \\ &  &  \\H_1(BG,\mathbb{Z}) & = & G/[G,G]\end{array}\right.$$
Since $Ch_*$ is an isomorphism and $\mu_G$ is assumed to be onto, the map $\iota$ is onto, which concludes the proof. $\blacksquare$
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
The classical Whitehead group of a discrete group $G$ is defined as $Wh(G):= K_1^{alg}(\mathbb{Z} G)/\langle\pm g: g\in G\rangle$, where $K_1^{alg}(\mathbb{Z} G)$ denotes the algebraic K-theory of the integral group ring of $G$. Define in a similar way the analytical Whitehead group of $G$ as $Wh^{an}(G):=K_1(C^*_r(G))/Im(\iota)$; then Conjecture \ref{Whitehead} is equivalent to the vanishing of $Wh^{an}(G)$ whenever $G$ has a 2-dimensional $BG$.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- def-7: body_md -->
\label{properaction} An action $G\curvearrowright X$ is {\bf proper} if for every point $x\in X$ there exists a $G$-invariant open neighborhood $U$ of $x$, a compact subgroup $H$ of $G$ and a $G$-equivariant continuous map $f_x:U\rightarrow G/H$.
<!-- end def-7 -->
<!-- ex-7: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
\item Any action of a compact group $G$ on any space $X$, is proper: take $U=X,\,H=G$ and $f_x$ the constant map to the one-point space.
\item Let $D_\infty$ denote the infinite dihedral group, i.e. the group given by the presentation
$$D_\infty=\langle s,t|s^2=t^2=e\rangle$$
(so that $D_\infty$ is the free product of two copies of $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$). Let $D_\infty$ act on the real line by setting $s(x)=-x$ (symmetry about 0) and $t(x)=2-x$ (symmetry about 1). There are now three cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item For $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$, we may take $U=\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Z}, \,H=\{e\}$; then, denoting by $U_x$ the connected component of $x$ in $U$, every connected component of $U$ is of the form $gU_x$ for a unique $g\in D_\infty$. So we may take as $f_x:U\rightarrow D_\infty$ the map that sends $gU_x$ to $g$.
\item For $x\in 2\mathbb{Z}$, assume first $x=0$. Then take $U=\mathbb{R}\setminus(2\mathbb{Z}+1)$ and $H=\langle s\rangle$. Denote by $U_{2n}$ the connected component of $U$ through $2n$; observe that there are exactly two elements $g\in D_\infty$ such that $gU_0=U_{2n}$, namely $g=(ts)^n$ and $g=(ts)^ns$. This defines the map $f_0:U\rightarrow D_\infty/\langle s\rangle$. For a general $x\in 2\mathbb{Z}$, just use conjugation.
\item For $x\in 2\mathbb{Z}+1$, assume first $x=1$, set $U=\mathbb{R}\setminus 2\mathbb{Z}$ and $H=\langle t\rangle$, and proceed analogously. 
\end{itemize}
\item For $G$ discrete, consider a covering $\begin{array}{l}X \\ \downarrow G \\Y\end{array}$ with group $G$: local triviality allows to write $X$ locally as $V\times G$, where $V$ is an open set in the basis $Y$. Here the action $G\curvearrowright X$ is both proper and free.
\item If $X$ is a CW-complex and $G\curvearrowright X$ is cellular, the action is proper if and only if stabilizers of vertices of $X$ are compact.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end ex-7 -->
<!-- def-8: body_md -->
\cite{BCH94} A {\bf universal example} for $G$-proper actions is a proper $G$-space $\underline{E}G$ such that for any proper $G$-space $X$ there exists a continuous $G$-equivariant map $f:X\rightarrow \underline{E}G$, and any two such maps are $G$-equivariantly homotopic.
<!-- end def-8 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{universal} A proper $G$-space $Y$ is a universal example for $G$-proper actions if and only if the two following conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every compact subgroup $H$ of $G$, the fixed point set $Y^H$ is non-empty.
\item Equip $Y\times Y$ with the diagonal $G$-action; let $p,p':Y\times Y\rightarrow Y$ denote the two projections. Then $p,\,p'$ are $G$-equivariantly homotopic.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
If $Y$ is a universal example, then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $H$ is a compact subgroup, then $G/H$ is a proper $G$-space, so there exists a $G$-equivariant map $f:G/H\rightarrow Y$. Since the coset $eH$ is $H$-fixed in $G/H$, we have $f(eH)\in Y^H$.
\item The diagonal $G$-action on $Y\times Y$ is proper. Since the maps $p,\,p'$ are $G$-equivariant, by the universal property of $Y$ they must be $G$-equivariantly homotopic. $\blacksquare$
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
If $H$ is any closed subgroup of $G$, then $\underline{E}G$ is a universal example for $H$-proper actions.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
Every locally compact, second countable group $G$ admits a universal example for $G$-proper actions.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- head-4: body_md -->
Define $\underline{E}G$ as the set of finitely supported probability measures on $G$, with the distance 
$$d(\mu,\nu)=\|\mu-\nu\|_\infty=\sup_{g\in G}|\mu(g)-\nu(g)|,$$
and the $G$-action by left translations. It is clear that this is a proper $G$-space. Let us check that it satisfies the two conditions in Proposition \ref{universal}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $H$ is a finite subgroup of $G$, then the uniform probability on $H$ is $H$-fixed.
\item For $0\leq t\leq 1$, the map $(\mu,\nu)\mapsto (1-t)\mu+t\nu$ provides a $G$-equivariant homotopy between $p$ (at $t=0$) and $p'$ (at $t=1$). $\blacksquare$
<!-- end head-4 -->
<!-- ex-8: body_md -->
\label{universalex}\begin{enumerate}
\item If $G$ is compact, then one may take $\underline{E}G$ to be a point. To anticipate on Example \ref{compactgroup}, in this case $K_0^G(\underline{E}G)=R(G)$, the additive group of the representation ring of $G$ (equivalently, the free abelian group on the dual $\hat{G}$); and $K_1^G(\underline{E}G)=0$.
\item If $G$ is a connected Lie group, let $K$ be a maximal compact subgroup of $G$ (recall that $K$ is unique up to conjugacy), we may take $\underline{E}G=G/K$. In particular, if $G$ is semi-simple with finite center, $G/K$ is the Riemannian symmetric space associated with $G$.
\item Let $F$ be a non-Archimedean local field (e.g. $F=\mathbb{Q}_p$, the $p$-adic numbers), and let $G$ be a semi-simple algebraic group over $F$ (e.g. $G=SL_n(F)$). Then we may take for $\underline{E}G$ the Bruhat-Tits building associated with $G$.
\item Let $G$ be a discrete torsion-free group, so that any proper action is also free. Denoting by $EG$ a contractible free $G$-space\footnote{Quoting from A. Connes: ``$EG$ is a point on which $G$ acts freely!''}, we may take $\underline{E}G=EG$.  Setting $BG:=EG/G$, we see that $EG$ is the universal cover of $BG$, so that $BG$ is the classifying space for $G$. Then $K_i^G(\underline{E}G)=K_i(BG)\,(i=0,1)$.
\item Let $G$ be a countable locally finite group, i.e. $G$ is a countable increasing union of finite subgroups $F_n$, say $G=\cup_{n\geq 0}F_n$. Then $\underline{E}G$ can be taken as a tree with vertex set $\coprod_{n\geq 0}G/F_n$ and edges of the form $\{gF_n,gF_{n+1}\}$, for $g\in G$. Observe that this tree fibers over $\mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end ex-8 -->
<!-- def-9: body_md -->
\label{Fred} An operator $T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ is a {\bf Fredholm operator} if the image $Im(T)$ is closed and the spaces $Ker(T)$ and $Coker(T):=\mathcal{H}/Im(T)$ are finite-dimensional. The {\bf index} of $T$ is then defined as $$Ind(T)=\dim_\mathbb{C} Ker(T)-\dim_\mathbb{C} Coker(T).$$
<!-- end def-9 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{AtiyahK0}(Atiyah) For $X$ compact, $K^0(X)\simeq [X,Fred(\mathcal{H})]$ as commutative monoids.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- ex-9: body_md -->
\label{circle} Take $M=S^1$ and $P=\frac{1}{i}\frac{d}{dt}$ acting on $L^2([0,2\pi],\frac{dt}{2\pi})$. In the trigonometric basis $e_k(t)=e^{ikt}\;(k\in\mathbb{Z})$, we have $P^2(e_k)=k^2e_k$ and $(1+P^2)^{1/2}(e_k)=(1+k^2)^{1/2}e_k$. Viewing $(1+P^2)^{1/2}$ as an order 1, invertible operator, we have:
$$\frac{P}{(1+P^2)^{1/2}}(e_k)=\frac{k}{(1+k^2)^{1/2}}e_k$$
and $\frac{P}{(1+P^2)^{1/2}}$ is a pseudo-differential operator of order 0. Then 
$$(1-(\frac{P}{(1+P^2)^{1/2}})^2)(e_k)=\frac{1}{1+k^2}e_k$$
so that $1-(\frac{P}{(1+P^2)^{1/2}})^2$ is a compact operator, and $\frac{P}{(1+P^2)^{1/2}}$ is Fredholm (of course of index 0, as it is self-adjoint).
<!-- end ex-9 -->
<!-- ex-10: body_md -->
\label{deRham} Let $M$ be a closed Riemannian manifold. Let $\Lambda^k T^*M$ denote the $k$-th exterior power of the cotangent bundle $T^*M$ (so that sections of $\Lambda^k T^*M$ are exactly $k$-forms on $M$). Set 
$$\Lambda^+ T^*M:=\oplus_{k\geq 0}\Lambda^{2k}T^*M;\;\Lambda^- T^*M:=\oplus_{k\geq 0}\Lambda^{2k+1}T^*M.$$
 Denoting by $d$ the exterior derivative on forms, define an operator $P:L^2(\Lambda^+ T^*M)\rightarrow L^2(\Lambda^- T^*M)$ by $P=d+d^*$. Then $P^*P=d^*d+dd^*$ is the Laplace-de Rham operator on differential forms, and $F:=P(1+P^*P)^{-1/2}$ is an elliptic pseudo-differential operator of order 0. Moreover
$$Ker(F)=\oplus_{k\geq 0}\{\mbox{harmonic $2k$-forms}\};\;Coker(F)=\oplus_{k\geq 0}\{\mbox{harmonic $(2k+1)$-forms}\}.$$
So $Ind(F)=\chi(M)$, the Euler-Poincar\'e characteristic of $M$.
<!-- end ex-10 -->
<!-- ex-11: body_md -->
Take $M=S^1$ and $P=\frac{1}{i}\frac{d}{dt}$ as in Example \ref{circle}. Then for $f,\xi\in C^1(S^1)$:
$$[P,f](\xi)=(Pf-fP)(\xi)=\frac{1}{i}((f\xi)'-f\xi')=\frac{f'}{i}\xi,$$
so that $[P,f]$ is pointwise multiplication by $\frac{f'}{i}$, which extends to a bounded operator on $L^2$, as it involves no differentiation anymore.
<!-- end ex-11 -->
<!-- exo-3: body_md -->
Check this for the operator $\frac{P}{(1+P^2)^{1/2}}$ of Example \ref{circle}.
<!-- end exo-3 -->
<!-- def-10: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a compact space. A triple $(\mathcal{H}^+,\mathcal{H}^-,F)$ is a {\bf Fredholm module} over $C(X)$ if
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathcal{H}^+,\mathcal{H}^-$ are Hilbert spaces which are modules over $C(X)$, i.e. there exists $*$-homomorphisms $\pi_\pm:C(X)\rightarrow\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^\pm)$.
\item $F:\mathcal{H}^+\rightarrow\mathcal{H}^-$ is a bounded, Fredholm operator.
\item For every $f\in C(X)$, the operator $F\pi_+(f)-\pi_-(f)F$ is compact.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end def-10 -->
<!-- def-11: body_md -->
\label{GFred} Let $X$ be a proper, $G$-compact space. A {\bf $G$-Fredholm module} over $X$ is a triple $(\mathcal{H}^+,\mathcal{H}^-,F)$ where:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathcal{H}^+,\mathcal{H}^-$ are Hilbert spaces equipped with (strongly continuous) unitary representations of $G$ and $G$-covariant representations $\pi_+,\pi_-$ of $C_0(X)$.
\item $F:\mathcal{H}^+\rightarrow\mathcal{H}^-$ is a linear, bounded, $G$-equivariant operator.
\item For every $f\in C_0(X)$, the operator $\pi_-(f)F-F\pi_+(f)$ is compact.
\item There exists a linear, bounded, $G$-equivariant operator $Q:\mathcal{H}^-\rightarrow\mathcal{H}^+$ such that for every $f\in C_0(X)$ the operators $\pi_+(f)(QF-1)$ and $\pi_-(f)(FQ-1)$ are compact.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end def-11 -->
<!-- def-12: body_md -->
\label{LHS} $$K_0^G(\underline{E}G):=\lim_{X\subset\underline{E}G} K_0^G(X)$$
where the limit is taken on the directed set of proper $G$-compact subsets $X$ of $\underline{E}G$.
<!-- end def-12 -->
<!-- ex-12: body_md -->
\label{equivpseudodiff} Let $M$ be a smooth, complete Riemannian manifold, and let $G\curvearrowright M$ be a proper, isometric, $G$-compact action. Let $E^\pm$ be $G$-equivariant smooth vector bundles over $M$, let $\mathcal{H}^\pm=L^2(M,E^\pm)$ denote their spaces of $L^2$-sections. Let $F:\mathcal{H}^+\rightarrow \mathcal{H}^-$ be a $G$-equivariant, elliptic, pseudo-differential operator of order 0. Then $(\mathcal{H}^+,\mathcal{H}^-,F)$ is a $G$-Fredholm module over $M$.
<!-- end ex-12 -->
<!-- ex-13: body_md -->
\label{equivdeRham} To get closer to Example \ref{deRham}, let us specialize Example \ref{equivpseudodiff} by taking $\mathcal{H}^\pm=L^2(\Lambda^\pm TM), P=d+d^*$ and $F=P(1+P^*P)^{-1/2}$. The operator $Q$ in Definition \ref{GFred} can be taken to be $Q=F^*$. The operator $QF-1=-(1+P^*P)^{-1}$ is not compact when $M$ is not compact, but it is ``locally compact'', meaning that $\pi_+(f)(QF-1)$ is compact for $f\in C_0(M)$. To see this latter point, we may assume that $f$ is compactly supported with support in an open chart of $M$, allowing us to replace $M$ by the $n$-torus $\mathbb{T}^n\;(n=\dim M)$. On $\mathbb{T}^n$ the desired compactness can be shown using Fourier series.
<!-- end ex-13 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{KKproduct} (Kasparov \cite{KasConsp}) There exists an associative, bi-additive product
$$KK_i(A,B)\times KK_j(B,C)\rightarrow KK_{i+j}(A,C):(x,y)\mapsto x\otimes_B y$$
(with indices counted modulo 2) that turns $KK_0(A,A)$ into a unital ring. Moreover any $*$-homomorphism $f:A\rightarrow B$ defines an element $[f_*]\in KK_0(A,B)$ such that $[f_*]\otimes_B y=f^*(y)$ for any $y\in KK_i(B,C)$. Similarly, if $g:B\rightarrow C$ is a $*$-homomorphism, then $x\otimes_B [g_*]=g_*(x)$ for every $x\in KK_i(A,B)$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- def-13: body_md -->
\label{KK0cycle} A {\bf cycle} for $KK_0(A,B)$ is a triple $(\mathcal{E}^+,\mathcal{E^-},F)$ where
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathcal{E}^\pm$ is a Hilbert $C^*$-module over $B$, equipped with a representation of $A$ given by a $*$-homomorphism $\pi_\pm:A\rightarrow\mathcal{L}_B(\mathcal{E}^\pm)$, and $F\in\mathcal{L}_B(\mathcal{E}^+,\mathcal{E}^-)$.
\item For every $a\in A$, we have $(F^*F-1)\pi_+(a)\in\mathcal{K}_B(\mathcal{E}^+)$ and $(FF^*-1)\pi_-(a)\in\mathcal{K}_B(\mathcal{E}^-)$.
\item For every $a\in A$, we have $F\pi_+(a)-\pi_-(a)F\in\mathcal{K}_B(\mathcal{E}^+,\mathcal{E}^-)$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end def-13 -->
<!-- ex-14: body_md -->
If $f:A\rightarrow B$ is a $*$-homomorphism, define $[f_*]=(B,0,0)$, where $B$ is viewed as a right $C^*$-module over itself, and as a left $A$-module through $f$. Then, since $\mathcal{K}_B(B)=B$, we see that all conditions in Definition \ref{KK0cycle} are satisfied.
<!-- end ex-14 -->
<!-- def-14: body_md -->
\label{KK1cycle} A {\bf cycle} for $KK_1(A,B)$ is a pair $(\mathcal{E},P)$ where
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathcal{E}$ is a Hilbert $C^*$-module over $B$, equipped with a representation of $A$ given by a $*$-homomorphism $\pi:A\rightarrow\mathcal{L}_B(\mathcal{E})$, and $P=P^*\in\mathcal{L}_B(\mathcal{E})$.
\item For every $a\in A$, we have $(P^2-P)\pi(a)\in\mathcal{K}_B(\mathcal{E})$.
\item For every $a\in A$, we have $[P,\pi(a)]\in\mathcal{K}_B(\mathcal{E})$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end def-14 -->
<!-- def-15: body_md -->
\label{homotopy} Two cycles $x_0,x_1$ for $KK_i(A,B)$ are {\bf homotopic} if there exists a cycle $y$ for $KK_i(A,B\otimes C[0,1])$ such that $e^{(0)}_*(y)$ is isomorphic to $x_0$ and $e^{(1)}_*(y)$ is isomorphic to $x_1$, where $e^{(t)}:B\otimes C[0,1]\rightarrow B$ denotes evaluation at time $t$.
<!-- end def-15 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{KKabelian} Equipped with direct sum, $KK_i(A,B)\;(i=0,1)$ is an abelian group.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- head-5: body_md -->
Any degenerate cycle for $KK_0(A,B)$ (resp. $KK_1(A,B)$) is homotopic to the trivial cycle $(0,0,0)$. Indeed (say $i=1$), let $x=(\mathcal{E},P)$ be a degenerate cycle for $KK_1(A,B)$. Then
$y=(\mathcal{E}\otimes C_0[0,1[,P\otimes 1)$ is a cycle for $KK_1(A,B\otimes C[0,1])$ (reason: since $\mathcal{K}_B(\mathcal{E}\otimes C_0[0,1[)=\mathcal{K}_B(\mathcal{E})\otimes C_0[0,1[$, we see that $y$ is a cycle because $x$ is degenerate). Since $e^{(t)}_*(y)=x$ for $0\leq t<1$ and $e^{(1)}_*(y)=(0,0)$, we see that $y$ provides the desired homotopy.
<!-- end head-5 -->
<!-- exo-4: body_md -->
Check the details of the previous proof.
<!-- end exo-4 -->
<!-- ex-15: body_md -->
(suggested by the referee) The ring structure on $KK_0(A,A)$ is not commutative in general. For example, $KK_0(\mathbb{C}^2,\mathbb{C}^2)$ is isomorphic as a ring to $M_2(\mathbb{Z})$.
<!-- end ex-15 -->
<!-- ex-16: body_md -->
\label{compactgroup} For $G$ compact and $A=\mathbb{C}$ with trivial $G$-action, we have $KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})=R(G)$, the representation ring of isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional representations of $G$. On the other hand $KK_1^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})=0$.
<!-- end ex-16 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{extension} Let $A,B,C$ be separable $G-C^*$-algebras. There exists a homomorphism 
$\tau_C:KK_i^G(A,B)\rightarrow KK_i^G(A\otimes_{min}C,B\otimes_{min}C)$ which is natural and compatible with the Kasparov product. For $i=0$ it is given by $(\mathcal{E}^+,\mathcal{E}^-,F)\mapsto(\mathcal{E}^+\otimes C,\mathcal{E}^-\otimes C,F\otimes 1_C)$, and analogously for $i=1$.
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- def-16: body_md -->
If $X$ is a proper, $G$-compact space, set
$$K_i^G(X):=KK_i^G(C_0(X),\mathbb{C})\;(i=0,1).$$
If $Y$ is any proper $G$-space (e.g. $Y=\underline{E}G$), set
$$K_i^G(Y)=\lim_X K_i^G(X)\;(i=0,1),$$
where the limit is taken on the directed set of proper $G$-compact subsets $X$ of $Y$.
<!-- end def-16 -->
<!-- ex-17: body_md -->
For $A=\mathbb{C}$ with the trivial $G$-action, we get $\mathbb{C}\rtimes G= C^*(G)$, the {\bf full group $C^*$-algebra}; and $\mathbb{C}\rtimes_r G=C^*_r(G)$, the reduced group $C^*$-algebra appearing in Conjecture \ref{BCconj}.
<!-- end ex-17 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
There exist natural {\bf descent} homomorphisms $$\widetilde{j_G}:KK_i^G(A,B)\rightarrow KK_i(A\rtimes G,B\rtimes G)$$ and $$j_G:KK_i^G(A,B)\rightarrow KK_i(A\rtimes_r G,B\rtimes_rG),$$
compatible with Kasparov products, such that the following diagram is commutative:
$$\left.\begin{array}{ccc}KK_i^G(A,B) & \stackrel{\widetilde{j_G}}{\longrightarrow} & KK_i(A\rtimes G,B\rtimes G) \\ & & \\j_G\downarrow&  & \downarrow(\lambda_{B,G})_* \\ & & \\ KK_i(A\rtimes_rG,B\rtimes_rG) & \stackrel{(\lambda_{A,G})^*}{\longrightarrow} & KK_i(A\rtimes G,B\rtimes_r G)\end{array}\right.$$
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{canon}\begin{enumerate}
\item There exists a non-negative $h\in C_c(X)$ such that $\int_G h(s^{-1}\cdot x)\,ds=1$ for every $x\in X$.
\item Set $p_X(x,s):=\sqrt{h(x)h(s^{-1}\cdot x)}$. Then $p_X$ is an idempotent in $C_c(X\times G)$ (endowed with twisted convolution as in (\ref{twisted}).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- ex-18: body_md -->
For $G=\mathbb{Z}$ acting by integer translations on $X=\mathbb{R}$, we may take $$h(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}x+1 & \mbox{if}\;x\in[-1,0] \\1-x & \mbox{if}\;x\in[0,1] \\0 & \mbox{otherwise}\end{array}\right. .$$
<!-- end ex-18 -->
<!-- def-17: body_md -->
$[p_X]$ is the {\bf canonical element} in $KK_0(\mathbb{C},C_0(X)\rtimes G)$.
<!-- end def-17 -->
<!-- def-18: body_md -->
For $B$ as above, the {\bf assembly map for $G$ and $B$} is the map $\mu_{G,B}:KK_i^G(\underline{E}G,B)\rightarrow K_i(B\rtimes_r G)$ given by $\mu_{G,B}:=(\lambda_{G,B})_*\circ\tilde{\mu}_{G,B}$.

\medskip
The {\bf assembly map} for $G$ is $\mu_G=(\lambda_G)_*\circ\tilde{\mu}_G:K_i^G(\underline{E}G)\rightarrow K_i(C^*_r(G))$.
<!-- end def-18 -->
<!-- conj-5: body_md -->
\label{BCcoeff} For every $C^*$-algebra $B$ equipped with a continuous $G$-action by $*$-automorphisms, the map $\mu_{G,B}:KK_i^G(\underline{E}G,B)\rightarrow K_i(B\rtimes_r G)\;(i=0,1)$ is an isomorphism.
<!-- end conj-5 -->
<!-- conj-6: body_md -->
\label{SNC} The map $\mu_G\circ\iota_*:K_i(BG)\rightarrow K_i(C^*_r(G))\;(i=0,1)$ is rationally injective.
<!-- end conj-6 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{(T)} If the non-compact, locally compact group $G$ has Kazhdan's property (T), then $(\lambda_G)_*:K_0(C^*(G))\rightarrow K_0(C^*_r(G))$ is not injective.
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- head-6: body_md -->
The group $G$ has property (T) if and only if there exists a projection $p_G\in C^*(G)$ such that, for every unitary representation $\pi$ of $G$, the projection $\pi(p_G)$ is the orthogonal projection of the subspace of $\pi(G)$-fixed vectors. Then
\begin{itemize}
\item Taking for $\pi$ the trivial one-dimensional representation $\epsilon$ of $G$, we get $\epsilon(p_G)=1$ which shows that $[p_G]$ has infinite order in $K_0(C^*(G))$.
\item Taking for $\pi$ the regular representation $\lambda_G$, which has no non-zero $G$-fixed vectors as $G$ is non-compact, we get $\lambda_G(p_G)=0$, completing the proof. $\blacksquare$
<!-- end head-6 -->
<!-- def-19: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a $G$-space. A {\bf $G-X-C^*$-algebra} is a $G-C^*$-algebra $D$ equipped with a $G$-equivariant homomorphism $C_0(X)\rightarrow Z(M(D))$ (the center of
the multiplier algebra of $D$) which moreover is non-degenerate, i.e $\overline{span(C_0(X)D)}=D$. The $G-C^*$-algebra $D$ is then {\bf proper} if there exists a proper $G$-space $X$ such that $D$ is a $G-X-C^*$-algebra.
<!-- end def-19 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{Tuproper} If $D$ is a proper $G-C^*$-algebra, then the map $\mu_{G,D}:KK_i^G(\underline{E}G,D)\rightarrow K_i(D\rtimes_r G)\;(i=0,1)$ is an isomorphism.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- head-7: body_md -->
There exists a proper $G-C^*$-algebra $D$ and elements $\alpha\in KK_i^G(D,\mathbb{C})$ (``the Dirac element'') and $\beta\in KK_i^G(\mathbb{C},D)$ (``the dual-Dirac element'') such that $\beta\otimes_D\alpha= 1_\mathbb{C}$ in $KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})$.
<!-- end head-7 -->
<!-- prop-11: body_md -->
\label{Strongass} Under Assumption (*), Conjecture \ref{BCcoeff} holds.
<!-- end prop-11 -->
<!-- def-20: body_md -->
\label{gamma} A {\bf $\gamma$-element} is an element $\gamma\in KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item There exists a proper $G-C^*$-algebra $D$, and elements $\alpha\in KK_i^G(D,\mathbb{C})$ (``Dirac element''), $\beta\in KK_i^G(\mathbb{C},D)$ (``dual-Dirac element'') such that $\gamma=\beta\otimes_D \alpha$.
\item For every compact subgroup $F$ of $G$, the image of $\gamma$ under the restriction map $Rest_G^F:KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})\rightarrow R(F)$ is the trivial one-dimensional representation $\epsilon_F$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end def-20 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{Tu}\begin{enumerate}
\item If a $\gamma$-element exists in $KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})$, then it is unique and moreover it is an idempotent in $KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})$.
\item Assume that a $\gamma$-element exists. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item For any $G-C^*$-algebra $B$, the map $\mu_{G,B}$ is injective. In particular the strong Novikov conjecture (Conjecture \ref{SNC}) holds. 
\item For a $G-C^*$-algebra $B$, the map $\mu_{G,B}$ is surjective if and only if the map $\otimes_{B\otimes_r G} \tau_{B\rtimes_r G}(\gamma)$ is the identity on $K_i(B\rtimes_r G)\;(i=0,1)$.
\end{enumerate}\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- ex-19: body_md -->
\label{Dirac} Let $M$ be a smooth, complete Riemannian manifold, and let $G\curvearrowright M$ be a proper, isometric, $G$-compact action. Take $\mathcal{H}^\pm=L^2(\Lambda^\pm TM), P=d+d^*$ and $F=P(1+P^*P)^{-1/2}$. Take moreover $D=C_0(M)$, a proper $G-C^*$-algebra. By Example \ref{equivdeRham} we have the element $\alpha=(\mathcal{H}^+,\mathcal{H}^-,F)\in KK_0(C_0(M),\mathbb{C})$, that we call the Dirac element associated with $M$.
<!-- end ex-19 -->
<!-- ex-20: body_md -->
\label{DualDirac} In the situation of Example \ref{Dirac}, assume moreover that $M$ is simply connected with non-positive curvature (so that $M$ is a model for $\underline{E}G$). By the Cartan-Hadamard theorem, any two points $x,y\in M$ are connected by a unique geodesic segment that we denote by $[x,y]$. Let $x_0$ be a base-point in $M$, set $\rho(x)=\frac{d_M(x_0,x)^2}{2}$, where $d_M$ denotes the Riemannian distance on $M$. Denote by $C_0(\Lambda^\pm TM)$ the set of continuous differential forms vanishing at infinity on $M$, and view it as a Hilbert $C^*$-module over $C_0(M)$. View the differential $d\rho$ as a 1-form and define the (unbounded) operator $P:C_0(\Lambda^+TM)\rightarrow C_0(\Lambda^-TM)$ as
$$P=ext(d\rho) + int(d\rho),$$
where (for $\omega\in C_0(\Lambda^+ TM)$):  $ext(d\rho)(\omega)=d\rho\wedge\omega$ and $int(d\rho)(\omega)$ is the contraction of the form $\omega$ on the gradient field $\nabla\rho$ of $\rho$. Then $P^*P$ is just pointwise multiplication by the function $\|d\rho\|^2=\|\nabla\rho\|^2$. But $\nabla\rho(x)$ is a tangent vector at $x$ to the geodesic $[x_0,x]$, pointing outwards from $x_0$, of norm $d_M(x_0,x)$. Hence $(1+P^*P)^{-1}$ is pointwise mutiplication by $\frac{1}{1+d_M(x_0,\cdot)^2}$ which is continuous and goes to 0 at infinity of $M$ and therefore defines a compact operator in the sense of $C^*$-modules.

For $g\in G$, the operator $gPg^{-1}$ is the similar operator defined with respect to the base-point $x'_0=gx_0$, using the function $\rho'(x)=\frac{d_M(x_0',x)^2}{2}$. 


\begin{figure}[h]
\centering

\node[point] at (xp0) {};

One checks that $\|\nabla(\rho-\rho')\|$ stays bounded on $M$: to see this, use the fact that the angle $\theta_x$ between $\nabla\rho(x)$ and $\nabla\rho'(x)$, goes to 0 when $x$ goes to infinity in $M$). As a consequence, defining $F=P(1+P^*P)^{-1/2}$, we may define the element $\beta=(C_0(\Lambda^+TM),C_0(\Lambda^- TM),F)\in KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},C_0(M))$ and we call it the dual-Dirac element.

This holds for example if $M$ is either a (finite-dimensional) Euclidean space of a Riemannian symmetric space of the non-compact type.
<!-- end ex-20 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
When $M$ is the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^n$, the operator $D^2$ is very much related to the harmonic oscillator operator on $\mathbb{E}^n$. Indeed, if $\omega$ is a $k$-form, we have (for $x\in\mathbb{E}^n$):
$$D^2\omega(x)=\Delta\omega(x)+\|x\|^2\omega(x)+ (2k-n)\omega(x).$$
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{gamma=1} In the setting of Examples \ref{Dirac} and \ref{DualDirac}, the equality $\gamma=1_{\mathbb{C}}$ holds when:
\begin{itemize}
\item $M=\mathbb{E}^n$ (see Kasparov \cite{KasConsp}).
\item $M=\mathbb{H}^n(\mathbb{R})$, the $n$-dimensional real hyperbolic space (see Kasparov \cite{KasLor}).
\item $M=\mathbb{H}^n(\mathbb{C})$, the $n$-dimensional complex hyperbolic space (see Julg-Kasparov \cite{JulKas}).
\end{itemize}
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{gammaexists} A $\gamma$-element exists for the following classes of groups.
\begin{itemize}
\item Groups acting properly on locally finite trees; here $\gamma=1_{\mathbb{C}}$ (see Pimsner \cite{Pimsner}).
\item Groups acting properly on locally finite Euclidean buildings (see Kasparov-Skandalis \cite{KaSk1}).
\item Hyperbolic groups (see Kasparov-Skandalis \cite{KaSk2}).
\item Groups with the Haagerup property (in particular amenable groups); here $\gamma=1_{\mathbb{C}}$ (see Higson-Kasparov \cite{HiKa}).
\end{itemize}
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- def-21: body_md -->
\label{(gamma)} Let $x=(\mathcal{H}^+,\mathcal{H}^-,F)$ be a cycle for $KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})$. We say that $x$ has {\bf property $(\gamma)$} if $\mathcal{H}^\pm$ carries a non-degenerate, $G$-equivariant representation $\pi_\pm$ of $C_0(\underline{E})$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every $f\in C_0(\underline{E})$, the function $g\mapsto F\pi_+(g\cdot f)-\pi_-(g\cdot f)F$ is in $C_0(G,\mathcal{K})$.
\item For every compact subgroup $F$ of $G$, the image of $\gamma$ under the restriction map $Rest_G^F:KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})\rightarrow R(F)$ is the trivial one-dimensional representation $\epsilon_F$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end def-21 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{nondeg} Let $\pi$ be a non-degenerate representation of $C_0(\underline{E})$ on $\mathcal{H}$.Then for every $f\in C_0(\underline{E}),T\in\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{H})$ we have $\lim_{g\rightarrow\infty}\|\pi(g\cdot f)T\|=0$.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $x$ is a cycle for $KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})$ with property $(\gamma)$, then $x$ is unique up to homotopy. Moreover $x$ defines an idempotent in the ring $KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})$ (as a consequence of uniqueness).
\item If $G$ admits a $\gamma$-element, then some cycle homotopic to $\gamma$ satisfies property $(\gamma)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{Shin}  Assume that there exists a cycle $x$ with property $(\gamma)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For any $G-C^*$-algebra $B$, we have $\nu_B^x\circ\mu_B=1_{KK_i^G(\underline{E},B)}$, so that $\mu_B$ is split injective. In particular the strong Novikov conjecture (Conjecture \ref{SNC}) holds.
\item If $x$ is homotopic to $1_{\mathbb{C}}$ in $KK_0^G(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C})$, then the Baum-Connes conjecture with coefficients (Conjecture \ref{BCcoeff}) holds for $G$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- ex-21: body_md -->
Let $X$ be either Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^n$ or a Riemannian symmetric space of the non-compact type. In this case, we know that there is a $\gamma$-element represented in the unbounded operator picture by the operator $D$ in formula (\ref{DdualD}), namely
$$D=d+d^*+ext(d\rho)+int(d\rho),$$
with $\rho(x)=\frac{d_M(x_0,x)^2}{2}$. Pass to the bounded picture by $F:=D(1+D^*D)^{-1/2}$. Then Nishikawa shows directly that the cycle $(L^2(\Lambda^+T^*M),L^2(\Lambda^-T^*M),F)$ has property $(\gamma)$. For this he appeals to the integral formula
$$F=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\infty D(1+D^*D+\lambda^2)^{-1}\,d\lambda,$$
based on the identity $\frac{s}{\sqrt{1+s^2}}=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{s}{1+s^2+\lambda^2}\,d\lambda$ for $s>0$.
<!-- end ex-21 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
\label{FPV1}(see \cite{FPV17}) The group $K_0^B(\underline{E}B)$ is naturally isomorphic to the free abelian group on the inductive limit of the system $(\widehat{B_n},s_n)_{n>0}$.
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- prop-14: body_md -->
\label{FPV2}(see \cite{FPV17}). Let $F$ be a non-trivial finite group, $B=F^{(\mathbb{N})}$.
\begin{enumerate} 
\item The free abelian group on $\hat{F}^{(\mathbb{N})}$ is naturally isomorphic to $K_0^G(\underline{E}B)$ with isomorphism given by
$$\pi\in\hat{F}^{(\mathbb{N})}\mapsto\otimes_{k\in Supp(\pi)}\pi_k\in R(\oplus_{k\in Supp(\pi)}F_k)\subset K_0^B(\underline{E}B).$$
\item The free abelian group on $Min(F)^{(\mathbb{N})}$ is naturally isomorphic to $K_0(C^*(B))$, with isomorphism given by
$$e\in Min(F)^{(\mathbb{N})}\mapsto \otimes_{k\in Supp(e)} e_k\in Min(\oplus_{k\in Supp(e)} F_k)\subset K_0(C^*(B)).$$
\item For $\pi\in\hat{F}^{(\mathbb{N})}$ we have $\mu_B(\pi)=\otimes_{k\in Supp(\pi)}\mu_F(\pi_k)\in K_0(C^*(B))$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-14 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
\label{lamplighter} (see \cite{FPV17})\begin{enumerate}
\item $K_0(C^*(L_F))$ is free abelian of countable rank, with an explicit basis consisting in projections from $C^*(B)$.
\item $K_1(C^*(L_F))=\mathbb{Z}$ generated by the class $[t]$ of $t$.
\item There exists a 2-dimensional model for for $\underline{E}L_F$ and $\mu_{L_F}$ is an isomorphism that can be explicitly described.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-15 -->
